docs.title: America needs Canada’s aluminum. Trump’s tariff exposed just how badly.
docs.text:
Global 
 America needs Canada’s aluminum. Trump’s tariff exposed just how badly.
 Ryan Dezember , The Wall Street Journal 10 min read 27 Oct 2026, 06:41 AM IST 
 Summary
 Smelters in Quebec run on cheap hydroelectric power. The Trump administration’s 50% tariff has pushed up prices for American industry. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 SAGUENAY, Quebec—When Nazi planes were blitzing London during World War II and the U.S. needed to build more aircraft and munitions in a hurry, it helped turn this remote place in the Canadian forest into an aluminum-production juggernaut.
 Thousands of Canadians labored through frigid conditions to build smelting pots and a hydropower plant to fuel them—in just 18 months. Ever since then, Saguenay’s aluminum plants have supplied American industry.
 Now, President Trump’s trade war has cast Canada’s aluminum smelters as the enemy—and U.S. businesses and consumers are paying a price.
 During his first term, Trump exempted Canada from a 10% aluminum tariff that he imposed on other trading partners. After he returned to the White House, he stripped Canada of its exemption and raised the tariff rate on aluminum to 50%.
 “They’ve treated the United States very unfairly,” Trump said last month about Canada. “They have been one of the worst countries in the entire world.” He has said the U.S. has no need for Canada’s natural resources.
 Aluminum has emerged as one of the trade war’s biggest conundrums. The steep tariff—imposed in the name of national defense—is intended to stimulate U.S. production. Yet the enormous power requirements for making aluminum have meant that Canada, where abundant hydropower has kept electricity prices from rising as sharply as in the U.S., has supplied about 70% of U.S. aluminum imports in recent years.
 The tariff has pushed aluminum prices in the U.S. to a record premium over global benchmarks, punishing home buyers, data-center developers, automakers and grocery shoppers. In addition to the new levy, trading restrictions on Russian metal and the Iran War, which choked off Persian Gulf exports, have contributed to global price increases.
 In Canada, Prime Minister Mark Carney is turning to Europe to forge new trade partnerships. The European Union’s top official said last month that she would work to add Canada as the trade bloc’s first associate member. Trump responded by threatening further tariffs on Europe and calling Canada “a terrible trade partner.”
 Alcoa, which dominated American aluminum production for decades, built the facilities upstream from the Saguenay Fjord, expanded them during World War II, then spun them off to meet antitrust rules. The hydropower stations, smelters, ore docks and other facilities are owned now by Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto.
 Rio, one of the largest aluminum producers outside China, is starting up in Saguenay the West’s first new smelters in more than a decade. The company also is working in Quebec to commercialize a new carbon-free smelting process in a joint venture with Alcoa and the provincial government, with support from the Canadian government and Apple.
 Much of the Canadian aluminum entering the U.S. comes from Rio’s Saguenay operation, which ships about 70% of its output across the border.
 “We always call aluminum ‘solid electricity,’” said Jérôme Pécresse, who runs Rio’s aluminum, lithium and Canadian businesses. “We cannot find a source of power in the U.S. which is anywhere close to what we have in Canada in terms of competitiveness.”
 In the U.S., Trump’s push for domestic smelting has met resistance.
 Emirates Global Aluminium, the Mideast’s largest producer, and Chicago-based Century Aluminum have said they would spend more than $4 billion to build what would be the largest U.S. smelter, capable of more than doubling domestic production of primary aluminum. The Biden administration awarded $500 million for the project, and Trump has thrown his support behind it with additional incentives.
 But opposition to the project has swelled in Inola, the Oklahoma prairie town chosen as the site. Local critics have expressed concerns about pollution and foreign ownership of land and objected to taxpayer-funded incentives to the developers.
 After a rowdy, marathon meeting in June where Trump officials promoting the smelter were heckled and booed, the Inola town council placed a moratorium on building permits and entitlements in its industrial park. Owners of property near the site sued in federal court seeking to block construction.
 The smelter became a divisive issue in Oklahoma’s Republican gubernatorial primary. Former state senator Mike Mazzei came out in favor of it and won Trump’s endorsement and the nomination. But he faced xenophobic political ads aimed at the project’s Mideast investors.
 “Mazzei wants to give your tax dollars to a Muslim country to build a smelter,” said the narrator in an ad made by a group called Put Oklahoma 1st. “Foreign workers, foreign landownership, threatening our way of life.”
 On a public call to rally support for Mazzei, Trump vouched for Emirates Global—“very fine people with unlimited money”—and said the smelter would bring jobs, tax revenue and the envy of other states.
 “This country desperately needs aluminum,” he said. “We get it all from Canada, for the most part, and we need it badly.”

 During the 20th century, the U.S. led the world in aluminum production.
 In 1886, Charles Martin Hall, a 22-year-old working in the woodshed behind his parents’ home in Oberlin, Ohio, had figured out how to mass produce it inexpensively using electric currents. Until then, aluminum had been so difficult to separate from its ore that it was more expensive than gold

Mint Money 
 Reel creators, drone shows and décor: the new costs of Indian weddings
 Ann Jacob 7 min read 27 Oct 2026, 12:41 PM IST 
 Summary
 Indian weddings are adding reel creators, drone shows and curated experiences to the bill. Couples are responding with DIY hacks, tighter budgets and financial planning to keep costs under control. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Earlier, a slideshow of pictures would tell guests how a couple met or trace their love story. Now, 200 drones might light up the night sky to map it out, while a dedicated social media crew edits and uploads Instagram reels in real time. Paint-and-sip stations, custom photo booths and curated guest activities are also finding their way into wedding venues.
 Over the past two to three years, Indian wedding budgets, once centred on venues, catering, décor and photography, have acquired new line items such as reel creators, drone shows, mixologists and interactive experiences. As these trends raise costs, couples are using do-it-yourself (DIY) ideas and financial planning to stay within budget.
 Reel creators, drone shows, and experiences
 “Weddings have changed quite a bit over the last few years. Earlier, most of the spending was around the venue, food, décor, and photography,” said Pradeep Chandar, creative director at Chennai-based Marriage Colours. “Now couples are looking at a lot more, like wedding content creators for instant reels, personalized guest experiences, welcome hampers, special entries, live entertainment, hospitality teams, and even separate budgets for pre-wedding celebrations.”
 Sahil Rathod, co-founder of Mumbai-based Shubhtithi Weddings, said dedicated social media vendors have emerged as a distinct expense. “Earlier, photographers used to edit the reels, but nowadays there are dedicated vendors for social media content creation who shoot reels, post live stories, and tag everyone,” he said. “While high-end teams charge ₹ 3-4 lakh for a two-day wedding, most couples comfortable with this trend spend around ₹ 1-1.5 lakh for 10-15 reels and live story coverage.”
 Drone shows and interactive stalls add to the bill. Chandar said some drone operators quote ₹ 6-10 lakh, while others advertise shows with 150-200 drones for ₹ 20 lakh. Digital projection mapping and LED installations are also replacing physical décor structures. Rathod said game stalls can cost ₹ 8,000 for simple setups and up to ₹ 50,000 for elaborate installations.
 Post-wedding dinners, reception mixologists and specialized hospitality managers are adding further costs, said Santosh Joseph, founder of Germinate Investment Services. “When it comes to offering these curated experiences, you end up paying for more people, managers, and specialized vendors,” he said.
 Chandar estimates that innovative experiences can increase wedding budgets in metro cities by up to 20%, with newer expenses ranging from ₹ 2 lakh to ₹ 20 lakh.
 DIY savings
 Some couples are countering these costs by doing more themselves. Teresa Chappala, a 30-year-old senior specialist in air imports from Mumbai, and her fiancé took charge of the creative work for their simple Christian wedding.
 “By dedicating our time and design skills, we managed to bypass heavy vendor premiums and cut down costs drastically without sacrificing the elegance of our wedding,” Chappala said.
 The couple made mirror prints for welcome boards, designed their wedding brochures, hand-made the bridal bouquet and built a photo booth. They also skipped a professional pre-wedding photography crew.
 “We did our entire pre-wedding shoot using a smartphone. The quality of mobile cameras nowadays is incredible, and the resulting photos feel far more authentic and intimate to us,” she said.
 They designed their own car décor and asked friends to help with venue logistics. “To use low-cost alternatives, you need to be ready to invest your own time. The small changes we made ended up making our wedding even more personal,” Chappala added.
 The couple completed their décor for ₹ 20,000, against vendors’ quotes of ₹ 50,000. Venue and catering costs remained unchanged.
 Cutting the extras
 For other couples, the financial battle lies in distinguishing genuine personal priorities from external social pressure. Pratap Khandulwan, a 26-year-old cybersecurity professional from Navi Mumbai, initially planned an intimate temple wedding with 25 to 30 close relatives. However, accommodating parental wishes pushed the estimated budget higher by over 80%.
 Khandulwan and his fiancé then decided which expenses mattered most. “We initially considered cinematic videos and drone shots too, but realized we didn't really need them. Just because something is trending on social media doesn't mean it has to be part of our wedding,” he said.
 The couple kept traditional rituals, pooja expenses and high-quality food as non-negotiables while trimming trendy extras. They opted for standard photography without videography, eliminated pre-wedding shoots, combined catering and decoration under a single contractor, and negotiated aggressively with venues.
 "Our biggest learning is that a wedding budget doesn't increase only because of luxury; sometimes it grows because of many seemingly small additions," said Khandulwan. The couple said they cut back on everyday discretionary spending and outings. "We want to travel, enjoy our married life, and create experiences beyond a single celebration rather than spend unnecessarily to match social expectations," he concluded.
 “For cost-conscious couples, research and knowing market value can go a long way,” Rathod said. He noted that most couples have shifted from physical to digital invitations and highlighted flexibility on dates as another major cost saver.
 “Couples flexible on dates can secure venues at lower rates or with major discounts during off-season periods,” he explained.

docs.text:
Mint Money 
 What will my hospital stay cost? Families deserve an answer in minutes
 Ajay Bakshi 4 min read 27 Oct 2026, 09:29 AM IST 
 Summary
 Hospitals treat a wide range of ailments with advanced technologies and a wide variety of medications, so a single bill can run into hundreds of line items. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 On 12 October, the Union health ministry asked every state to make hospitals display their prices. It is a welcome step, but not enough. A hospital's rate card can list 2,000 prices, and a family in a crisis cannot make head or tail of it—nor does a list tell them what their final bill will be.
 As a clinician and former hospital chief executive, I have seen why. Hospitals treat a wide range of ailments with advanced technologies and a wide variety of medications, so a single bill can run into hundreds of line items. And all the labour, materials and equipment used must be captured and fed to the billing system in real time—without errors. Families expect (almost demand) a narrow estimate. But each patient is unique, and even for common procedures, complications can and do happen.
 Many hospitals solve this with packages—a hernia surgery package, for example, covering the room, the surgery, the medicines and some specific tests. But a diabetic patient needs more tests, a patient with heart failure needs care from the cardiology team, and an unexpected complication (an allergy to a medicine, say) lengthens the stay. Off-the-shelf packages cannot capture every scenario, and families perceive any variation from the estimate as dishonesty.
 Transparency is key
 Transparency generates trust, but only transparency that a family can use. A family should be able to take a recommendation from a trusted doctor and get price quotes for exactly that treatment from 10 hospitals—within minutes, and all online. That needs two steps.
 First, a treatment recommendation from their doctor in four standardized parts: the treatment (medical or surgical), the expected length of stay, any high-value implants or devices, and the patient's known conditions (diabetes or heart failure, for example). The hospital's software, not the doctor, would code the treatment in the Central Government Health Scheme ( CGHS ) code list of October 2025, which covers about 2,000 services—the vast majority of what tertiary care hospitals do.
 CGHS would serve as a common language and a base coding system, not a price cap. The recommendation would belong to the patient in their digital health record.
 Second, each hospital publishes its own price in rupees for each of these codes (by room category where it applies), in a format that apps can read, and keeps it current. How a hospital sets those prices remains its own business. A family will rarely read this list. Their app will.
 Medicines and consumables are harder. Hospitals bill them at the printed maximum retail price (MRP), and the amounts they pay their suppliers are commercially confidential. Rather than reveal their margins, hospitals should publish what their prices exclude, the MRP of high-value implants and devices, and an indicative range of what medicines and consumables have typically added to the bill for each code. A planned hernia repair can be estimated closely. A patient admitted with heart failure can only be given a range because no doctor can predict on day one how long that patient will need intensive care.
 The same two steps work for insured patients. The rates hospitals negotiate with insurers are confidential and need not be published. An insured family can upload its coded recommendation into the insurer's app. And the insurer, which already holds those rates, can show its policyholder the likely co-payment, room-rent eligibility and use of the sum insured at each network hospital—without revealing the rates to anyone else.
 With these inputs, third-party apps and insurers can turn a treatment recommendation into a rupee estimate for every hospital, and a new ecosystem will grow around what doctors and hospitals publish. If a doctor at a second hospital changes the plan, that hospital must explain the reason in writing before admission.
 It is a win-win. Hospitals retain the freedom to set their own prices, and families (cash or insured) receive comparable estimates within minutes, which they can use to make an informed decision about which hospital to select. Other factors, such as the quality of care, the doctors, customer friendliness and additional facilities, will help hospitals differentiate themselves beyond pricing.
 The 12 October letter was a good first step. The next step is for the government to enforce meaningful price transparency and support an independent information ecosystem to help families make informed decisions, without regulating prices.
 Dr Ajay Bakshi is a neurosurgeon and former chief executive of three Indian hospital chains: Max Healthcare, Manipal Hospitals and Gleneagles Hospitals.

News Cent raises $15 million to scale preventive health screening business Rwit Ghosh 3 min read 27 Oct 2026, 04:00 PM IST Summary Bengaluru-based preventive health startup Cent raised $15 million in a Series A round led by Blume Ventures and South Park Commons. It plans to invest in research, AI radiology and screening technology, and expand from three centres to 7–10 across Bengaluru, Mumbai and Gurugram by mid-2027. Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Subscribe now Preventive health screening startup Cent has raised $15 million in a Series A funding round comprising equity and debt, led by Blume Ventures and existing investor South Park Commons, the company announced on Tuesday. The round also saw participation from individual investors, including Arun Sarin, former chief executive of Vodafone, and Srinivas Narayanan, former chief technology officer of OpenAI’s business-to-business division, among others. “Most of the equity raise is going towards improving our research and development,” said co-founder Anshul Khandelwal in an interview with Mint . “This means that we'll be building out our bioinformatics platform which combines molecular biology, structural data, functional data, dynamic data, clinical data.” The Bengaluru-based Cent was founded by Khandelwal alongside Practo co-founder Shashank ND and Arpit Garg. The company raised its first round of capital in March—a $5 million seed cheque from South Park Commons and Shashank's family office, OneFlow Holdings. Cent operates centres that offer full body screenings to find previously undetected cardiac, cancer , neuro, and metabolic conditions in individuals. The startup's fundraise comes at a time when Indian consumers are increasing their spending on preventive health, fitness, and wellness. GenZ's spending on fitness and wellness is expected to grow to $40 billion by 2030, up from $11 billion in 2024, according to a joint report by Redseer and Fireside Ventures published in November 2025. Similarly, Millennials are expected to spend $39 billion on fitness and sports by 2030, up from $21 billion in 2024. Apart from its bioinformatics platform, the company is investing in two other areas. One is enhancing Medsee, an artificial intelligence -based radiology platform it recently acquired. The terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. “We'll be developing this further to make sure radiologists can reporter faster and report more accurately,” Khandelwal said. The company is also investing in developing hardware for preventive health screening at its centres, as well as devices that can be used at home. While Khandelwal declined to get into details, he said that some of the products under consideration included wearable devices, as well as a “new way of scanning at the centre itself.” Offline expansion Cent currently operates three centres across Bengaluru, Mumbai and Gurugram. The debt component, which the company described as a very small portion of the fundraise, will be used to finance capital expenditure for expanding its centres across these three cities. “Bengaluru was profitable from day one, since it was the first one we launched. Mumbai is currently profitable. Gurgaon was launched three months later, so it's on the path to profitability,” said Khandelwal. “Each of these can do around $5-6 million in revenue a year.” The company plans to expand the number of centres to 7-10 by mid-2027. Cent has no plans immediately to expand to more geographies, and is instead opting to have 5-6 centres across the three cities it currently operates in. “Once we're done with these, we go to Pune, Chennai, Hyderabad. India has the potential to have at least 100 centres,” Khandelwal said. Cent charges ₹ 25,000 for a single screening, which takes around three hours. Consumers must also undergo a genomics test, taking the total cost of screening at its centres to ₹ 30,000-35,000 per person. According to the company, the tests generate up to 7-8 gigabytes of biological data per individual, covering nearly 300 conditions across the human organ systems. The company also offers a follow-up screening six months after the initial test. Gift this article Check your portfolio About the Author Rwit Ghosh Rwit is a correspondent at Mint covering India’s burgeoning startup ecosystem and the venture capital and private equity firms that back them. Sitting out of Bengaluru, he writes on the new-age tech businesses that the city and the rest of the country seems to continuously be birthing.

While Rwit’s interests lie in covering the new wave of deeptech, AI, SaaS and consumer tech businesses, he’ll write on consumer brands and fintech (if someone repeatedly explains these sectors to him).

When he’s not scrolling through the Indian startup forums on Reddit, Rwit is usually trying to figure out early signs of what’s to come next in the ecosystem. As a result, he’s been early to spot trends like VCs becoming more active in backing deeptech, funding bottlenecks for agentic AI startups and a potential revival in edtech through AI.

Prior to his ongoing stint at Mint, Rwit worked at NDTV Profit as a social media producer while also working on his own stories for the TV channel after he graduated from the Asian College of Journalism in Chennai.

When he’s not working on stories, he can be found trying to figure out where he should go to eat next in Bengaluru, or what his next tattoo should look like. If you see him in the wild, you should ask him how he pronounces his name. He’s definitely not tired of being asked about it. docs.title: Homebuyer stops EMIs after builder resells flat; K'taka HC quashes SBI’s case — ‘Outstanding loan not criminal offence’
docs.text:
Delivering a key ruling on borrower rights, the court observed that an outstanding financial liability cannot automatically be treated as a criminal offence.
According to an Economic Times (ET) report, in the financial year 2019-20, Mr Bari took a ₹ 39.92 lakh home loan from SBI to purchase a flat (B-306) in Bengaluru’s Grandeur Park project. He reportedly signed a standard tripartite agreement with the bank and the developer on 8 February 2020.
Because he lived in Mumbai , Bari could not regularly inspect the site, but he consistently paid his Equated Monthly Instalments ( EMIs ).
However, Bari later discovered the builder had sold his allotted flat to a third party in March 2023 without informing him or SBI . In response, Bari immediately stopped his EMI payments.
Instead of solely pursuing the builder, SBI filed an FIR against Bari in September 2024, accusing him of cheating, criminal breach of trust, and misappropriating the loan amount.
Citing clauses 2,4, 5 and 6 of the tripartite agreement, SBI’s lawyers said that if the builder has cancelled the booking due to Bari defaulting or the project getting shelved, then the builder is legally obliged to repay the bank any money received from Bari.
Under Clause 5 of the agreement, the builder was explicitly mandated to refund the entire amount collected from the homebuyer directly to the bank if the project fails to materialise.
Quashing the FIR against Bari, the Karnataka High Court noted that the homebuyer never received the property title, took no part in the resale, and gained no financial benefit from the builder's fraudulent transaction.
The court strongly criticised the bank's approach, stating that a public-sector institution is expected to exercise due care before invoking criminal proceedings against a customer.
“The existence of an outstanding loan or the failure of the underlying transaction, by itself, cannot be treated as constituting a criminal offence,” the court observed, emphasizing that criminal prosecution cannot be used as a shortcut for civil financial recovery unless there is clear malicious intent.
However, the ruling does not resolve the question about what happens to Bari’s booking and the money paid towards the property, since the court was dealing with the criminal case proceedings.
Kalpit Khandelwal, Partner at Aekom Legal, told ET that the agreement explicitly made the builder—not the buyer—liable to repay the bank if the project failed. Because Bari exhibited no dishonest intent, the court correctly classified the dispute as a civil recovery matter.
He advised homebuyers to carefully scrutinise their tripartite agreements, as these contracts dictate who bears the financial risk if a builder defaults or a housing project stalls.

 American bosses are desperately trying to de-MAGAfy
 The Economist 1 min read 27 Oct 2026, 08:53 PM IST 
 Summary
 Many bosses have abandoned that even-handedness over the past two years. Companies identified a window of opportunity to advance their agendas. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 American bosses once acted on the knowledge that, in politics, the wheel always turns. Parties came in and out of power, and so companies curried favour with both Republicans and Democrats regardless of who controlled the White House or Capitol Hill.
 Many bosses have abandoned that even-handedness over the past two years. Companies identified a window of opportunity to advance their agendas, says Reggie Babin of Akin, a lobbying shop. Since Donald Trump’s return to power, pushing through long-desired mergers or securing regulatory changes has often meant abandoning bipartisanship—and dignity, judging by the many corporate donations to Mr Trump’s garish new ballroom.
 In a few days, however, the president is predicted to emerge from the midterm elections with a far weaker grip on Washington. Accordingly, much of corporate America has been desperately trying to scrub off its spray tan and deflate its lip filler. But rebuilding ties with the Democrats will not be easy.
 One way this shows up is in the people businesses appoint to handle government relations. In January 2025, the same month Mr Trump was inaugurated, Meta elevated Joel Kaplan, its longtime Republican-whisperer, to be the social-media giant’s chief emissary. On October 20th it announced that Mr Kaplan will be leaving the company. Paramount Skydance, which recently completed its takeover of Warner Bros Discovery with the president’s blessing, has hired a former staffer from the Biden administration to help court the Democrats. Other companies that have enlisted former Democratic aides in the past six months include Palantir, a maker of data-analysis tools, as well as Polymarket and Kalshi, two prediction markets.
 The tilt away from Mr Trump can also be seen in America Inc’s donations. Companies are barred from giving candidates money from their own coffers. But they can co-ordinate donations by setting up political action committees (PACs), which solicit voluntary contributions, mostly from company executives. Those executives can also give to candidates directly or through trusts.
 The Economist examined federal filings covering donations by business leaders and their families across these channels. In the second quarter of 2026, the latest period for which data are available in full, 33% of their giving went to Democrats, up slightly from 31% across 2025. Yet that vastly understates the shift, as a disproportionate share of mega-donors support Republicans. Strip out the ten biggest—including Elon Musk—and 51% of donations in the second quarter went to the Democrats, up from 36% throughout last year.
 For the most part, America Inc still draws the line at supporting socialists. Of the $287m that executives donated to Democrats in the first half of this year, a mere $9m has gone to progressives, including those endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America. Take out the donations given by Saikat Chakrabarti, most of which went to the entrepreneur’s own unsuccessful primary bid, and the figure drops to just over $4m.
 America’s bosses, however, may find that even moderate Democrats have become unreceptive to their overtures. Stopping data centres is not the only anti-corporate rallying cry that has pervaded the midterms. In Iowa, big agriculture is the villain; in Alaska, it is big fish. One former Democratic official sums up the party’s new outlook on corporate America bluntly: “We demand blood.”
 In Silicon Valley the nervousness is palpable. Chris Hughes, a co-founder of Facebook and friend of the Democrats, notes that many tech bosses spent much of the past two years “running around Washington” trying to shape regulation in their interests. One venture capitalist predicts “a reckoning” after the midterms for those who cosied up to Mr Trump. “History is not going to look back particularly favourably on those who leaned in.”
 Sensing the threat, some have gone on the attack. Consider the contest for a Senate seat in Ohio. Sherrod Brown, the Democratic candidate seeking to return to the Senate, is a vocal critic of the crypto industry. Fairshake, its flagship PAC network, is thus spending $55m in a bid to prevent his comeback. But some prominent industry figures—including Chris Larsen, co-founder of Ripple, a crypto-infrastructure provider—have opposed the effort, worrying that it will create animosity with Democratic lawmakers, and that Mr Brown is unlikely to forget the attacks if he wins. Mr Larsen has donated through other channels to the Democrat’s campaign.
 Capitol punishment
 The blue wave may end up smaller than polls suggest. But even if the Democrats take the House only narrowly and lose the Senate, they will be able to give businesses a headache. Control of the lower chamber would give Democratic committee chairs the power to subpoena company files and call executives to testify. That could cause embarrassment, or worse.
 Washington lawyers say they have been fielding calls since the start of this year about potential investigations. In some cases, they have already been hired to parse employees’ actions and communications for indiscretions that could become public, and have been working to pick and train telegenic witnesses from their clients’ ranks. Edward O’Callaghan of Cahill, one law firm, says he has been counselling some businesses to pre-emptively meet influential members of Congress in a bid to avoid public hearings. Where Democratic support seems unlikely, they can instead prepare Republicans with favourable information to use in a hearing.

 The winners and losers of Trumponomics
 The Economist 4 min read 27 Oct 2026, 09:02 PM IST 
 Summary
 America’s economy is indeed growing briskly, with output on course to expand at an annualised rate of around 3% in the third quarter. But many of those Mr Trump claimed he would help have lost out, while richer Americans have gained. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.

 ALL POPULISTS promise much to the working man, but Donald Trump predicted a golden age. Just before the election in 2024, he told voters they were days away from “the best jobs, the biggest paychecks, and the brightest economic future the world has ever seen”. His unorthodox blend of tariffs, tax cuts and deportations, he claimed, would bring down living costs, revive America’s industrial heartland and restore middle-class prosperity.
 Has the president delivered? On October 22nd the White House claimed his policies were driving up wages and fuelling a “blue-collar BOOM”. America’s economy is indeed growing briskly, with output on course to expand at an annualised rate of around 3% in the third quarter. But many of those Mr Trump claimed he would help have lost out, while richer Americans have gained.
 The most politically toxic policies are those that have raised daily costs. The president’s sweeping tariffs have pushed up the cost of consumer goods by roughly 2%, according to the New York Fed. The Budget Lab at Yale estimates they will cost the average household $1,100 this year. The war in Iran has also sent oil prices soaring, and is set to add another $1,000 to the average household’s costs by year’s end.
 Pushing in the other direction, Mr Trump’s flagship tax-and-spending law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, has boosted tax refunds by around $340 on average. The law also created “Trump accounts”, an effort to broaden ownership in the stock market, with eligible newborns entitled to $1,000 to invest in shares. But the law’s biggest gains went to richer Americans, through lower taxes, even as it tightened access to food stamps—with more than 5m Americans losing benefits so far—and to Medicaid, the health-care programme for the poor.
 To tally the net effects of these gains and losses, The Economist combined estimates of the impact of tariffs, higher petrol prices and Mr Trump’s tax-and-spending law across income groups in 2026. We estimate that Mr Trump’s policies will cost the poorest tenth of American households, with average income after taxes and transfers of around $37,000, almost 3% of their income. The richest tenth, with average after-tax incomes of nearly $500,000, will gain nearly 3% (see chart 1). Households in the middle, with average income of roughly $100,000, lose more than $400. That does not account for the effect of a decision, taken by Congressional Republicans last year and endorsed by Mr Trump, to let enhanced Obamacare subsidies expire. That has raised average premiums for individual insurance purchased on exchanges by nearly $800 a year, according to KFF, a health-policy research group.
 Housing costs pose another problem for the president. Mortgage rates, pushed up in part by the inflationary effects of his war in Iran, have climbed above 7%, prompting existing owners to stay put. Adding new supply has become more costly. Last year builders estimated that tariffs on materials would add nearly $11,000 to the cost of a typical new home. His immigration crackdown is fuelling labour shortages, too; in September a survey from the National Association of Home Builders reported that labour costs were up by 4.2% from a year earlier. It is lower-income and middle-class voters, again, who are most pinched. In May sales of starter homes fell by 5.4% from a year earlier, even as luxury-home sales rose by 6.2%, according to Zillow, an online property firm.
 When it comes to jobs, health care and social assistance have accounted for almost all private-sector gains since January 2025, to meet demand from America’s ageing population. The artificial-intelligence boom has been another bright spot, with data-centre investment creating roughly 180,000 new jobs in industries related to the build-out. In other sectors, though, private employment has barely budged. Annual wage growth across the private sector has slowed from 4% to 3%; rising inflation means that workers’ hourly pay is 0.7% lower in real terms than a year ago. Labour’s share of nonfarm business output has fallen to its lowest level since records began in 1947 (technical changes to how business owners’ earnings are classified explain only some of the decline).
 A renaissance in manufacturing jobs has been particularly elusive. Though manufacturing output has risen, manufacturing employment has fallen by some 20,000 since January 2025, while factory workers’ wages have failed to keep pace with inflation over the past year. In North Carolina, which Mr Trump won in 2024 and which now looks set to elect a Democrat to the Senate, nearly 9,000 factory jobs have disappeared over the past year.
 Americans invested in the stock market have more to celebrate, as the AI bonanza has driven up the value of the S&P 500. But the impact is, once again, lopsided. Of the $17trn increase in Americans’ equity and mutual-fund wealth since the end of 2024, nearly 90% accrued to the richest tenth of households, compared with just 0.6% for the poorer half, according to data from the Federal Reserve (see chart 2).
 These phenomena have not gone unnoticed. Nearly two-thirds of Americans think that Mr Trump’s economic policies have made conditions worse, according to a recent survey by the Pew Research Centre; the same is true of 35% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents, nearly twice the share in January. ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund on Monday launched a new fund offer (NFO) for the ICICI Prudential BSE Power ETF, an open-ended Index Exchange-Traded Fund that tracks the BSE Power Index. It gives subscribers exposure to the entire power value chain — across generation, transmission, integrated utilities and heavy electrical equipment, the company said in an official release.
“India’s power sector is at an important juncture, with rising electricity consumption, expanding industrial activity and large-scale infrastructure development creating opportunities across the power value chain. With the launch of ICICI Prudential BSE Power ETF, investors can access a diversified basket of companies across this value chain through a single investment,” Vipin Bhandari, Head – Retail Business, ICICI Prudential AMC said in the release.
ICICI Prudential BSE Power ETF — All you need to know
 NFO close date: The NFO, which opened on Monday, 26 October will close on Friday, 30 October.
The release added that MICR cheques will be accepted till up to 30 October, while e-payments and RTGS requests will be accepted till the end of business hours up to 30 October 2026.Portfolio allocation: Exposure to the entire power value chain as the BSE Power Index comprises constituents of BSE 500 Index that are classified as per the following Basic Industries as defined in the common India Industry Classification Structure — Heavy Electrical Equipment, Power Generation, Integrated Power Utilities, Power-Transmission, Power Trading, Power Distribution and Other Electrical Equipment.Expected returns: Notably, the BSE Power Index has delivered a CAGR of 20% over five years, 17% over three years and 8% over one year. Data as on 30 September, showed, the release said.The statement noted that the power sector has growth potential, with electricity demand up more than 5× since 2000, and as GDP and urban centres expand. India’s installed capacity is projected to rise from 596 GW (2025) to 1,154 GW (2034), marking a CAGR of 7.24%, driven by strong government policy, industrial expansion, and diversified generation mix, it added.Stock cap and weighing: Index constituents are weighted by their float-adjusted market cap, subject to an individual stock weight cap of 25%.Why BSE Power Index? Covering BSE 500 companies across heavy electrical equipment, power generation, integrated power utilities, power transmission, power trading, power distribution and other electrical equipment, the index has 17 constituents and they are weighted by free-float market capitalisation, subject to an individual stock weight cap of 33% and a basic industry weight cap of 30%.In terms of sectors, utilities make up 59.59% of the index and industrials the remaining 40.41%. By market capitalisation, the index has a large-cap tilt with 75.57% large caps and 24.42% mid-caps. The top ten constituents together account for 78.90% of the index. The index is reconstituted semiannually in June and December and rebalanced quarterly.Who are the managers? The ETF will be managed by Nishit Patel, Ashwini Bharucha and Venus Ahuja, according to the statement.What is the estimated risk level? The scheme is classified as ‘very high risk’, as per the release.Exit Load: NilMinimum Application Amount: During NFO ₹1,000 and in multiples of Re 1.Minimum Investment Amount (Post Allotment): On stock exchanges investors can buy/sell units of the Scheme in round lot of 1 unit and in multiples thereof.While directly with the MF, authorised participant(s) / investor(s) can buy or sell units of the scheme in creation unit size viz. 32,000 units and in multiples thereof.Disclaimer: This story is for educational purposes only.  TVS family feud: Venu Srinivasan, son and wife along with daughter file caveats
 Varun Sood , Satish John 5 min read 28 Oct 2026, 05:40 AM IST 
 Summary
 TVS Motor Co. chairman-emeritus Venu Srinivasan, son Sudarshan Venu, wife Mallika Srinivasan, and daughter Lakshmi Venu have filed a total of eight caveats in two Chennai courts 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The feuding family members of the TVS Group have filed a slew of caveats in Chennai courts, as an ownership dispute hangs over the Chennai-based business conglomerate. TVS Motor Co. chairman-emeritus Venu Srinivasan, son Sudarshan Venu, wife Mallika Srinivasan, and daughter Lakshmi Venu have filed a total of eight caveats in two Chennai courts, a Mint review of court records showed.
 On 12 October, Venu Srinivasan filed the first, naming Lakshmi and Mallika Srinivasan in the City Civil Court. The same day, Mallika Srinivasan filed a caveat, naming Venu and Sudarshan. All four family members also filed caveats in the Commercial Court the same day. Lakshmi Venu also filed a caveat in the City Civil Court the next day, naming her father, while Sudarshan filed a case against his sister.
 The caveats ensure that the court hears a party before passing any order over a petition moved by the rival party. In the TVS family dispute, the father and son are ranged on one side, and the mother and daughter on the other.
 The caveats were filed three days after Mint reported on 9 October that Mallika and Lakshmi were seeking "a fair settlement" over the assets of the TVS Group, as patriarch Venu Srinivasan was reported to have given much of the ownership to son Sudarshan Venu.
 “Is this (filing a caveat) a precursor to this ownership dispute going to court? One cannot say for sure,” said an executive who works with Mallika Srinivasan. “Every effort is being made to resolve this amicably. But both sides need to be open to settling,” said the executive, declining to elaborate.
 Emails sent to Venu Srinivasan and Mallika Srinivasan seeking comment went unanswered.
 “As stated earlier in their joint statement, Dr Lakshmi Venu and Mallika Srinivasan reiterate their desire for an amicable resolution through transparent discussions and dialogue,” a spokesperson for the two said.
 Split and after
 The wider TVS business was divided between Venu Srinivasan and his cousins in 2020. Four years later, Venu Srinivasan and his family members signed another family agreement, under which his son, Sudarshan, and daughter, Lakshmi, were given control of two public companies: automaker TVS Motor and die-casting company Sundaram-Clayton Ltd. Under this agreement, Venu Srinivasan and Sudarshan control TVS Holdings, the main holding company of TVS Motor Company. They also control the privately owned financial services and real estate business, according to a Mint review of the 2024 Memorandum of Understanding.
 Srinivasan and Lakshmi control Sundaram-Clayton Ltd, the listed die-casting company. Venu Srinivasan wields control over TVS Motor and Sundaram-Clayton. Mallika and Lakshmi separately control Tractors and Farm Equipment Ltd (TAFE).
 The 2024 family agreement is now facing a challenge—Mallika Srinivasan says it was only about managing the businesses, non-compete clauses and using the brand, and did not split ownership of the businesses among the children, the fourth generation of TV Sundaram Iyengar, the founder of the 115-year-old TVS industrial group.
 “No economic settlement has taken place within the Venu Srinivasan family,” Mallika, chairperson and managing director of Tractors and Farm Equipment Ltd (TAFE), told Mint on 13 October, in her first on-record telephone interview on the dispute. “I do believe that the legitimate economic interests of both children must be recognized fairly and equitably,” she said.
 The dispute comes at a time when Venu Srinivasan wields considerable influence over the Tata Group, the country’s largest conglomerate. His support for Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran for a third five-year term and his backing to make the Group company public are at the centre of a conflict with most of the Tata Trustees, including chairman Noel Tata.
 Stake tangle
 TVS family members own 59.09% of Sundaram-Clayton. VS Trust, with Venu Srinivasan as sole trustee, owns 46.83%, while a family branch owns 6.87% through TSF Investments Ltd. Srinivasan holds 4.38% personally, and Mallika and Lakshmi own 0.26% and 0.75%.
 TVS Holdings owns 56% of TVS Motor. The family holds 74.45% of TVS Holdings: VS Trust owns 66.55%, Srinivasan Trust (with VS Trustee Private Ltd as trustee) owns 3.07%, and the family branch owns 3.74% through TSF Investments. Mallika and Lakshmi own 0.29% and 0.82%.
 As the sole trustee of VS Trust, Srinivasan controls voting power in both companies. Lakshmi may run Sundaram-Clayton, but her direct shareholding is less than 1%.
 TVS Holdings Ltd had a market cap of ₹ 23,217 crore at the end of Tuesday, while TVS Motor was valued at ₹ 1,93,778 crore and Sundaram-Clayton at ₹ 2,361 crore.

docs.title: RBI EDF form: Is export declaration mandatory for all service exporters, freelancers, YouTubers? Expert explains
docs.text: The RBI released the amended Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026, on September 22, which came into effect on October 1, 2026.According to the regulations, “an exporter of services shall furnish to the specified authority, a declaration in EDF specifying the amount representing the full export value of services, within 30 days from the end of month in which invoice for services has been raised.”Exporters of services other than software are required to submit the EDF on or before the date they receive payment. The new rules have raised questions about who needs to file the Export Declaration Form (EDF), how the process works, and what charges banks can levy. Here’s what an expert has to say.What is the Export Declaration Form (EDF)?Rohan Sewani, Head of Operations & Customer Experience at Skydo, said the Export Declaration Form (EDF) is a declaration an exporter gives their bank. It lists the exports made and the money they expect to receive for them.The bank uploads it to RBI’s Export Data Processing and Monitoring System (EDPMS). The entry stays open against the exporter’s PAN until the payment comes in and the bank matches it.Until now, export reporting under EDPMS was largely relevant to goods exports and certain software exports. From October 1, the requirement has expanded to a wider range of service exporters, including those providing software, consulting, marketing, design and other services to overseas clients, he added.What is the deadline to file the EDF form?Sewani said the EDF must be submitted within 30 days from the end of the invoice month. The first submission deadline is 30 November 2026 for invoices raised during October.Exporters can consolidate their monthly invoices into one EDF to simplify the process, although filing separate declarations for different invoices is also permitted.Another important change is the time allowed to bring export proceeds into India. It has been shortened from 15 months to nine months, and from 18 months to 12 months for exports invoiced or settled in Indian rupees, effective 1 October. This realisation deadline is separate from the EDF filing deadline, he explained.What is the step-by-step process for filing an EDF?Sewani explained that service exporters required to file an EDF should follow these steps:Start by organising the export invoices raised during the month. Each invoice should contain the overseas client's details, invoice number, date, currency, amount, and description of services.Identify the correct Services Accounting Code (SAC) for their services and the AD code of the bank branch where they hold their account. The form also requires the exporter’s IEC, GSTIN and PAN, contract reference and net realisable value for each invoice.The next step is to prepare the declaration using these details. Service exporters need to complete Part 1, covering general information, and Part 2B, covering the export value of services. They also need to identify the type of payment, including whether it is an advance or non-advance payment.The filing deadline is 30 days from the end of the invoice month. For invoices raised in October 2026, the deadline is 30 November 2026. Exporters can also submit their declarations earlier.The authorised dealer bank then records the declaration in RBI's Export Data Processing and Monitoring System (EDPMS). When the corresponding payment is received, the inward remittance information is matched with the export declaration, allowing the bank to reconcile and close the entry.For invoices up to ₹10 lakh, the entry can be closed on the exporter’s own declaration that the payment has been received.Is EDF filing mandatory for freelancers and YouTubers?Sewani said the new EDF requirement covers a much wider range of service exporters. Large IT companies that previously filed SOFTEX forms have now moved to the EDF framework.However, the RBI Governor’s clarification on October 7 indicated that individuals undertaking transactions of a personal nature would be exempt. Clarity on whether all freelancers qualify for this exemption is still awaited through the RBI’s FAQs.Covered: Companies, LLPs, partnership firms, agencies, IT and SaaS businesses, and global capability centres billing overseas clients.Likely exempt: Individuals earning in a personal capacity. This includes freelancers, tutors, and YouTubers or creators receiving Google AdSense payouts in their own name, subject to RBI’s FAQs.Grey area: sole proprietors with GST, Udyam/MSME, or other business registrations.“In practice, banks are currently applying this differently. Some have stopped asking individuals for an EDF, while others are still asking for it regardless of whether the exporter is a registered business,” he added.What fees can banks levy and what do RBI rules say?Sewani said the RBI has not prescribed a fixed fee or cap for EDF filing. Under the 2026 export regulations, banks can charge for handling export transactions, but the charges must be reasonable and proportionate to the service provided.Since some banks are charging per EDF, consolidating a month’s invoices into one declaration may help exporters keep costs down. If a charge appears excessive, exporters can raise the issue through the bank’s grievance redressal process and, if unresolved, approach the RBI Ombudsman, he added.

Jio Platforms shares trade at 22% premium in grey market ahead of IPO debut
 Strong investor demand and a resilient grey market premium fuel expectations of a blockbuster listing for Mukesh Ambani's digital giant
 Jio Platforms’ IPO attracted over $78 billion in bids, with its grey market premium holding at around 22% ahead of its October 28 debut.
 Bloomberg 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 11:49 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 For investors lucky enough to land shares in Jio Platforms Ltd.’s $3.1 billion India-record initial public offering, trading on the unofficial market is fueling hopes of a big debut pop. 
 Billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s digital and telecommunications giant has attracted stellar demand across investor categories ahead of its Oct. 28 market debut. Investors who got their allocations on Tuesday are now closely watching Jio’s gray-market pricing for clues about how the first day might unfold. The premium over the IPO price has hovered at about 22% for roughly 10 days, unusually resilient for an offering of this size, according to the ipowatch.in and investorgain.com platforms. 
 Gray market premiums are unregulated and provide no guarantee of where a stock will actually trade once it hits the exchange. Still, they are widely tracked in India as a barometer of demand and listing-day sentiment. 
 If the pattern holds into the listing, it would make Jio India’s second-most valuable company after parent Reliance Industries Ltd., pushing rival Bharti Airtel Ltd. into third place. That prospect is adding to the excitement around an IPO that’s already rewritten records in India’s capital markets. Jio attracted more than $78 billion in bids and nearly 14 million applications in one of the country’s most anticipated listings. 
 So far, Jio has been able to defy the usual trend of gray market premiums cooling after an IPO closes, as the initial rush of bidding fades and investors shift their focus to allotments and the eventual listing. After National Stock Exchange of India Ltd.’s $2.4 billion IPO, the premium gradually eroded from about 15% to 3% in two weeks and the shares ultimately made a relatively muted debut.
 The optimism is backed by blockbuster subscription numbers. Jio’s IPO was subscribed more than 22 times, with qualified institutional buyers bidding for 71 times the shares reserved for them. Wealthy investors subscribed 14 times their allocation, while the retail portion was covered 2.7 times. The offering was fully subscribed within just 100 minutes of opening last week, even as a bruising selloff swept through Indian equities.

Infosys draws four downgrades in a day on weaker annual sales outlook
 Brokerages turn cautious as Infosys' reduced FY27 sales guidance raises concerns over demand recovery and AI-led disruption
 Infosys shares fall after the company cuts its FY27 revenue growth forecast, prompting a wave of analyst downgrades. (Photo: Reuters)
 Bloomberg 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 11:56 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 By Faseeh Mangi 
 Infosys Ltd. was downgraded by at least four analysts in a single day after India’s second-largest software exporter cut its annual sales forecast, deepening concerns over disruption from artificial intelligence. 
 Axis Capital Ltd., Arihant Capital Markets Ltd., and IIFL Capital Services Ltd. were among brokerages that lowered their ratings on Monday, data compiled by Bloomberg show. Three others reduced their recommendations over the weekend, pushing its consensus rating to 3.7 out of 5, the lowest since January 2024. 
 The downgrades for the sector’s bellwether threatens to derail a nascent recovery in India’s battered technology shares. The Nifty IT Index is on track for its best month since July, even as concerns mount over soaring debt levels being used to fund the global AI buildout. 
 Infosys cutting its annual sales forecast signals that a broad-based recovery in IT budgets has yet to materialize. Revenue will rise 1% to 2% on a constant-currency basis in the year through March 2027, the company said late Friday, versus analysts’ estimates of just over 2%. 
 India’s $280 billion-plus software services industry has been grappling with a slowdown, with companies limiting spending in the midst of geopolitical crises such as the Iran conflict, surging energy prices and elevated inflation. 
 Infosys shares have fallen 28% this year on ongoing concerns about its ability to weather AI disruption. The average target price from 44 analysts is 1,200 rupees. The stock tumbled about 3% to 1,132.2 rupees in early trading on Tuesday.

Discounted valuations offset near-term headwinds for Tata Consumer
 Tata Consumer Products reports 14% revenue growth and 16% profit growth in Q2FY27, with strong performance in growth businesses and expectations of margin expansion in the second half
 premium 
 TCPL has generated double-digit revenue growth across segments (except tea) for the last five quarters
 Devangshu Datta New Delhi 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 28 2026 | 12:11 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Tata Consumer Products Ltd (TCPL) on Monday reported its results for the second quarter of financial year 2026-27 (Q2FY27), which met or exceeded consensus. Consolidated revenue was up 14 per cent year-on-year (Y-o-Y) at ₹5,661 crore, with India volume up 11 per cent Y-o-Y. TCPL has taken price hikes of 8-10 per cent in many products in FY27 to date. The portfolio mix is changing with a focus on growth areas.
 TCPL has generated double-digit revenue growth across segments (except tea) for the last five quarters. The portfolio is pivoting to high-growth segments like Sampann, Soulfull, Ready to Drink (RTD), Capital Foods, Organic India, etc. This should accelerate revenue growth. TCPL launched 22 new products in Q2FY27. 
 The gross margin contracted 41 basis points (bps) Y-o-Y and 99 bps quarter-on-quarter (Q-o-Q) to 41.7 per cent due to input-inflation. But the company’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation (Ebitda) grew 17 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹780 crore, with margin expansion of 31 bps Y-o-Y to 13.8 per cent. India A&P (advertising and promotion) spends were 5.5 per cent of sales in Q2, and 5.8 per cent in the first half (H1) of FY27. Interest costs reduced 23 per cent Y-o-Y, pushing up profit before tax (PBT). The reported profit after tax (PAT) grew 16 per cent to ₹470 crore, while adjusted PAT after exceptional items was up 18 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹480 crore.
 TCPL offers premium pulses, dry fruits, breakfast cereals, snacks, RTD beverages, and cold-pressed oils, but tea and salt are the largest components. Salt is moving up the value-chain through a process of formalisation, while tea is a seasonal seller. Salt contributes 20 per cent to TCPL's revenue; its Q2FY27 revenue grew 15 per cent Y-o-Y while volumes rose 9 per cent. TCPL has taken a price hike of 6 per cent in salt in early October (adding to 6 per cent hike in June). The impact would be visible in Q3FY27.
 The growth businesses portfolio (which includes Tata Sampann, RTD beverages, Capital Foods, and Organic India) grew sales by 40 per cent Y-o-Y in Q2FY27, contributing 38 per cent to India business revenue. Sampann sales expanded 57 per cent Y-o-Y, while RTD volume grew 34 per cent with value up 47 per cent Y-o-Y. Capital Foods grew by over 18 per cent Y-o-Y, and Organic India grew by over 9 per cent Y-o-Y. Both Sampann and RTD categories grew volumes despite high bases of above 30 per cent in Q2FY26. TCPL has reiterated guidance for over 30 per cent value growth in these fast-track businesses over the next two-three years.
 The management says it is focused on operating profit margin (OPM) expansion of 50-70 bps in FY27, and expects margins to expand from current levels due to price hikes and peak seasons for India tea and US coffee. Also Sampann margins have risen 280-290 bps Y-o-Y to over 14 per cent, and international margins are also expected to rise. TCPL thinks the India OPM can cross 17 per cent in next three years.
 Tea volume was flat Y-o-Y, while revenue declined 1 per cent. TCPL took a price hike of 6 per cent in early October to meet inflation. In the international segment, beverage sales grew 7 per cent Y-o-Y (down 2 per cent in constant currency, or CC). In CC, while US coffee grew at 6 per cent Y-o-Y, the UK was down 8 per cent, and Canada was up 8 per cent.
 The management expects mid-single-digit volume growth for tea and salt, alongside pricing hikes across both portfolios. Better margins are likely in the second half (H2) of FY27, as tea sees gains in autumn and winter seasons. The festive season should push demand for Capital Foods. The margin guidance of 50-70 bps gain in FY27 is based on these assumptions. In terms of raw material costs, robusta and arabica prices may soften, improving US coffee margins. The Soulfull segment grew 23 per cent last year, and targets 25-30 per cent growth in FY27. In the quick-commerce (qcom) category, Sampann portfolio items are in top positions.
 TCPL has introduced AI in the Himalayan factory to do online bottling inspection. It is using AI-led guidance about tea to assess crop situation, temperature, and heat, and to provide timing recommendations on when to buy. It is also using AI for invoice validation.
 The company has an impressively consistent growth profile. The key risks include volatility in commodity prices, weather-related changes in demand, and disruptions to export routes. The stock has corrected substantially over the past 12 months. This makes valuations more attractive, and analysts now seem to have reached a bullish consensus. docs.title: Is Vodafone Idea a Buy now? Jefferies outlines 3 scenarios with up to 143% upside
docs.text: Can a stock that has fallen 23% still hold a big surprise? Global investment bank Jefferies has kept a ‘Buy’ rating on Vodafone Idea (Vi). However, it has cut its target price to Rs 16 from Rs 20. That still means a 34% rise from the current market price. The eye-catcher, though, is an upside scenario that points to 143% gain potential from current levels. Its upside scenario analysis also presents a more optimistic price target of Rs 29 while the downside scenario projects possibility of the price falling to Rs 9. What could determine which direction the stock takes? Vodafone Idea: Jefferies outlines 3 scenarios, 3 possible outcomes The brokerage has mapped three possible paths. According to the Jefferies report, Vodafone Idea’s valuation depends heavily on how much telecom tariffs rise over the next few years and how quickly the company can improve its earnings. ScenarioTarget pricePotential returnBase caseRs 1634%Upside caseRs 29143%Downside caseRs 9-25% In its base case, Jefferies assumes a single 15% tariff hike in April 2027. It expects revenue and cash EBITDA to grow at compound annual growth rates (CAGRs) of 11% and 25%, respectively, between FY26-29. ALSO READElon Musk’s Starlink is at India’s Door. 4 Sectors That Could Feel it First The upside case assumes cumulative tariff hikes of 25% between FY27-29. Under this scenario, the brokerage values the stock at Rs 29, implying a potential gain of 143%. But if tariffs remain unchanged over the same period, its downside scenario places the target at Rs 9, indicating a possible fall of 25%. Vodafone Idea: Why has Jefferies retained its 'Buy' rating? Vodafone Idea’s share price has corrected 23% from its September levels. According to Jefferies report, the outlook for its FY2028 EBITDA remains unchanged in consensus estimates. The improvement in subscriber trends is an important part of the investment case. The Jefferies report noted that the network expansion has helped stabilise subscriber trends. The company increased its broadband base stations by 39% and network sites by 14% over the past two years. Jefferies expects Vodafone Idea’s network sites to increase by 26% to 2,61,000 by FY29. Tariff hikes could make a significant difference Higher mobile tariffs are central to Jefferies’ optimistic outlook. The report noted, “Given VIL's high operating leverage (~20% cash EBITDA margins), we estimate every 10% tariff hike drives a 17% increase in its cash EBITDA.” It also noted that Vodafone Idea’s enterprise value-to-market capitalisation ratio is 2.2 times. Is Vodafone Idea cheap compared with its past valuations? Valuation is another factor behind the brokerage’s call. The telecom player, Vodafone Idea is trading at around 21 times its enterprise value to cash EBITDA, below its five-year average, according to Jefferies. The brokerage believes the valuation could remain elevated until earnings growth strengthens and cash EBITDA margins improve to above 40%. It expects these levels to be achievable around FY32-33. Jefferies also estimates that the company could deliver an annualised return of 16% through March 2032, assuming a 12-times valuation multiple on its FY2033 cash EBITDA. This is a longer-term estimate, not a guaranteed return. ALSO READVi allows pan-India data sharing in new prepaid family plan What investors need to watch The biggest uncertainty is whether the company can implement tariff increases while keeping subscribers. Jefferies added “VI's fair value ranges between Rs 9-29/share, implying 143% upside potential and 25% downside potential”. The report noted, “We lower our target multiple to 20x EV/EBITDA due to higher yields and reiterate 'Buy' with lowered price target of Rs 16” Disclaimer: This article is based on research reports from one or more brokerage firms and is for informational purposes only. The views, target prices, and recommendations expressed are those of the respective brokerage firms and do not reflect the official policy or position of Financial Express. This should not be construed as an offer, solicitation, or recommendation to buy or sell securities. Investors must conduct their own independent due diligence and seek advice from a SEBI-registered financial advisor before making any investment decisions.

docs.title: 6 ‘Buy’ recommendations by Jefferies with 34% to 63% upside
docs.text: Jefferies sees opportunities across real estate, power transmission, cement, banking and oil refining, with six 'Buy'-rated stocks backed by company-specific growth drivers and improving business prospects. The brokerage’s preferred picks include companies expanding their project pipelines, strengthening cash generation, improving operating performance or benefiting from favourable industry conditions. Godrej Properties and Adani Energy Solutions feature prominently on the list, supported by expectations of stronger cash flows and sustained earnings growth. JK Cement’s capacity expansion plans and IndusInd Bank’s potential profitability recovery also support Jefferies’ view. For Bharat Petroleum Corporation, refining performance remains a key earnings driver, while Au Small Finance Bank’s growing deposit franchise and transition to a universal bank form important parts of its investment case. Jefferies on Godrej Properties: 'Buy' Jefferies has a 'Buy' on Godrej Properties, with a target price of Rs 2,550, implying an upside potential of 63%. In its October 23 report, the brokerage pointed to improved collections, stronger operating cash generation and a healthy project launch pipeline. Collections rose 31% year on year in the September quarter, while the operating cash flow surplus more than doubled. Jefferies sees scope for stronger pre-sales in the second half of FY27 as new projects come to market. The company’s management raised its FY27 pre-sales guidance to Rs 39,200 crore to Rs 41,700 crore, implying growth of 15% to 22% year on year. Jefferies expects stronger cash generation to support positive free cash flow in the second half of FY27 and through FY28. It also considers management’s FY28 target of a 20% reported return on equity achievable. The brokerage’s assessment rests on the company’s ability to convert its project pipeline into sales and cash collections, while maintaining growth over the coming financial years. “Strong launch pipeline near term could drive a guidance beat taking pre-sales growth to 20%+,” Jefferies said. The company’s capacity expansion programme remains central to its longer-term plans. The North India expansion is expected to take cement capacity to around 40 million tonnes per annum in the first half of FY28. Further brownfield projects are intended to support its target of reaching 50 million tonnes of capacity by FY30. Its investment case rests on volume growth, planned capacity additions and the company’s ability to manage operating costs as it expands. docs.title: Tata Consumer soars 6% after Q2: Why brokerages cut target prices by nearly 14%
docs.text: The Tata Consumer Products share price surged over 6% in early trade on Tuesday, October 27 after the company’s results for the second quarter of financial year 2027 (Q2FY27) met the Street’s expectations. Brokerages have maintained their positive outlook on the company but flagged some concerns around margins in its India business due to rising commodity costs. Global investment bank Jefferies retained its ‘Buy’ rating while brokerage JM Financial maintained its ‘ADD’ rating. Tata Consumer Q2 earnings Tata Consumer Products on Monday reported a 16% year-on-year (YoY) increase in consolidated net profit to Rs 469 crore for Q2FY27, in line with Street estimates. Its revenue from operations rose 14% YoY to Rs 5,661 crore in Q2, exceeding Bloomberg consensus estimates of Rs 5,583 crore for the quarter. ALSO READ7x earnings, a 59% fall: Vijay Kedia and Dolly Khanna’s latest smallcap bets The company’s consolidated earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) rose 16.6% YoY to Rs 783 crore for the quarter. Its EBITDA margin was 13.8% in Q2, compared with 13.5% a year earlier, also in line with street estimates. Jefferies on Tata Consumer: Riding the Quick Commerce wave The global investment bank Jefferies has maintained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock but reduced the price target by 14% to Rs 1,250. This implies an upside of 33% from the stock’s closing price of Rs 936.5 on Monday. Tata Consumer remains among the investment bank’s top picks in the sector. Tata Consumer’s Q2FY27 revenue growth exceeded Jefferies’ estimates, with the India-branded underlying volume growth of 11% being “impressive”. The earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) margins of this segment contracted YoY due to inflationary pressures in tea and salt. However, the company has increased prices of its products, which should help expand margins from Q3FY27 onwards. The company remains a key beneficiary of the rapid rise of quick commerce, especially for its growth portfolio, which contributed around 38% of the India business in Q2, Jefferies said. The company’s management retained its margin expansion guidance of 50-70 basis points in FY27 as the benefit of price hikes comes through. It expects tea volumes to pick up, and also retained the guidance of over 30% growth for the growth portfolio. JM Financial on Tata Consumer: India ops margin recovery key Brokerage JM Financial maintained its ‘ADD’ recommendation on the stock but reduced the target price by 13% to Rs 1,065 apiece. This implies an upside of around 14%. The brokerage said the pace of recovery in margins of India business will be the key factor to watch hereon. “We have cut FY27E/28E by 1–3%, factoring lower margins. We have trimmed target multiple to 43x (52x earlier) given the broader sector derating and volatility in margin delivery; roll forward valuation to Sep’28E to yield a revised TP of INR 1,065 (earlier INR 1,225). Following a +18% correction in the past three months, valuations are below their long-term average and restrict further downside,” the brokerage said. ALSO READZomato: Agentic AI fear overblown? Brokerages reaffirm ‘Buy’ with up to 38% upside JM Financial said the revenue trajectory shall remain resilient going forward, led by the growth business, salt business and pricing-led recovery in domestic tea. It expects margins to also improve as the full benefits of the price hikes in tea and salt will be seen in Q3FY27, and with stable international or non-branded business profitability. Tata Consumer: India margin recovery remains key While the company posted firm numbers for the September quarter, margin pressure was visible for its India business. The management expects margins to recovery gradually as the full benefit of price hikes pass through to consumers. docs.title: 5 Buy recommendations by Nomura, with 25% to 63% upside potential
docs.text: Nomura has identified five stocks with potential upside of 25% to 63.2%, led by Sterlite Technologies, according to its research reports dated October 26, 2026. Aditya Birla Real Estate, Ather Energy, Jindal Steel and ITC Hotels complete the list, ranked by their implied upside to Nomura’s target prices. The brokerage has a ‘Buy’ rating on all five stocks. Nomura on Sterlite Technologies: 'Buy' Nomura has set a target price of Rs 1,350 for Sterlite Technologies, implying an upside of 63.2% from current levels. The brokerage’s investment case centres on demand for optical and digital connectivity infrastructure, including data-centre connectivity. Sterlite Technologies reported strong second-quarter FY27 results, with revenue rising 145% year on year to Rs 2,529 crore and EBITDA increasing 405% to Rs 651 crore, according to Nomura’s report. The brokerage values the company at 30 times its estimated December 2028 earnings per share. Risks include a slowdown in artificial intelligence data-centre capital expenditure, faster-than-expected commissioning of industry capacity, weaker operating income and execution, and higher cash outflows from legal claims. Nomura’s report discusses the company’s demand outlook and execution risks, including the challenges associated with data-centre projects. Nomura on Aditya Birla Real Estate: 'Buy' Nomura has set a target price of Rs 1,600 for Aditya Birla Real Estate, implying an upside of 48.4% from current rate. The brokerage values the company using a sum-of-the-parts approach that accounts for the net asset value of its residential project pipeline, annuity assets and untapped land bank. Its valuation also includes a premium based on the company’s growth potential. Aditya Birla Real Estate reported pre-sales of Rs 300 crore in the second quarter of FY27, down 67% year on year and 10% quarter on quarter. Collections, however, rose 48% year on year to Rs 750 crore. Nomura’s report identifies execution of projects linked to the Worli land parcel and delays in FY27 launches as key downside risks. ALSO READ7x earnings, a 59% fall: Vijay Kedia and Dolly Khanna’s latest smallcap bets The company’s ability to execute planned launches and convert its development pipeline into sales will be important to the brokerage’s valuation case. Nomura on Ather Energy: 'Buy' Nomura has set a target price of Rs 2,070 for Ather Energy, implying an upside of 31.4% from current levels. The brokerage raised its target price from Rs 1,926 after the electric two-wheeler maker reported better-than-expected average selling prices and margins in the second quarter of FY27. Revenue reached Rs 1,460 crore, up 63% year on year, while EBITDA margin came in at 0.8%, compared with Nomura’s estimate of a 2.6% loss margin. ALSO READL&T to BEL, HAL: 12 defence stocks in focus after DAC clears Rs 2.12 lk cr procurement Ather’s bookings and customer enquiries also grew strongly, while the company raised its planned annual production capacity to 1.14 million units by the second quarter of FY28. Nomura sees the launch of the new Konarc range as an additional growth opportunity. “We reaffirm Ather as our top pick in the 2W space,” Nomura said. The brokerage said Ather’s technology, expanding reach and product portfolio position it well to benefit as electric vehicles gain importance in the two-wheeler market. Nomura on Jindal Steel: 'Buy' Nomura has set a target price of Rs 1,300 for Jindal Steel, implying an upside of 28.2%. The brokerage maintained its rating and target price after the company reported second-quarter FY27 consolidated EBITDA of Rs 2,504 crore, beating Nomura’s estimate by about 15%. The result was supported by improved realisations and a higher share of flat steel products in the sales mix. Consolidated volumes rose 27% year on year to 2.4 million tonnes. Realisation per tonne increased 12% year on year and came in 4% above Nomura’s estimate. However, conversion costs rose 7% quarter on quarter, driven by higher power, fuel and freight expenses. “The beat on our estimate was on account of higher-than-expected realization,” Nomura said. The brokerage’s target price is based on an enterprise value-to-EBITDA multiple of 8.5 times. Jindal Steel’s production ramp-up and planned capacity additions remain important factors in its outlook, while higher raw material and operating costs could weigh on profitability. Nomura on ITC Hotels: 'Buy' Nomura has set a target price of Rs 205 for ITC Hotels, implying an upside of 25%. The brokerage’s investment case includes the company’s plans to expand its hotel portfolio through owned and managed properties. Expansion across both models can help the company grow its room base while using different approaches to ownership and operations. “We like the company’s strategy of owned/ managed hotel key expansion,” Nomura said. The target price places ITC Hotels fifth among the five stocks in this list by implied upside. The brokerage’s view rests in part on the company’s ability to expand its hotel network and execute its growth plans. Conclusion The five picks span sectors ranging from digital connectivity and electric mobility to real estate, steel and hospitality. Sterlite Technologies leads Nomura’s list on potential upside, while the other four stocks offer exposure to different business growth drivers. Whether these targets are achieved will depend on companies delivering on expansion plans, sustaining operating performance and managing sector-specific risks.
