 Fujiyama Power Systems Ltd, a solar energy solutions provider specialising in rooftop solar systems, saw its shares rise nearly 3% on Tuesday, October 27. The small-cap solar stock is in focus as brokerage firm Motilal Oswal has shared its outlook on the company, highlighting its planned expansion into advanced solar cell manufacturing and battery energy storage systems.
Fujiyama Power Systems shares advanced 2.68% to Rs 373.65 at 3:30 pm on the NSE. The stock's gains come as investors assess the company's growth prospects in India's expanding rooftop solar market and its plans to strengthen manufacturing capabilities. Its proposed expansion into solar cell production and energy storage could create additional growth opportunities over the coming years.
Motilal Oswal has reiterated its Buy rating on Fujiyama Power Systems with a target price of Rs 500. From the current price of Rs 373.65, the target indicates a potential upside of approximately 33.8%.
The brokerage expects the company to deliver a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 52% in revenue, 57% in EBITDA and 59% in adjusted profit after tax between FY26 and FY28. In its report, Motilal Oswal said, "We expect UTLSOLAR to clock a CAGR of 52%/57%/59% in revenue/EBITDA/ adj PAT during FY26-28. We reiterate our BUY rating with a TP of INR500, based on 20x FY28E EPS."
The target price is based on 20 times the brokerage's estimated FY28 earnings per share. These projections depend on the company's ability to execute its expansion plans and deliver the anticipated improvement in profitability.
A key growth driver is Fujiyama's planned 1.2GW TOPCon solar cell manufacturing facility at Ratlam, Madhya Pradesh. TOPCon is an advanced solar cell technology designed to improve solar panel efficiency. Commercial production at the facility is expected to begin in the first half of FY28.
The project forms part of the company's backward integration strategy, which involves manufacturing more components in-house rather than relying entirely on external suppliers. This could strengthen domestic sourcing, improve cost control and support the production of solar cells that meet domestic content requirements.
Motilal Oswal believes China's proposed restrictions on the overseas transfer of certain advanced solar manufacturing technologies are unlikely to disrupt the project, as Fujiyama has already secured a technology transfer agreement from China.
The brokerage also sees opportunities in Fujiyama's battery energy storage system (BESS) business. The company has installed a 5MW storage system at Dadri and plans an additional 10MW system at Ratlam.
Battery storage allows electricity to be stored for use when required and can complement solar installations for commercial and industrial customers. Fujiyama could use its existing rooftop solar portfolio and distribution network to expand into integrated solar-plus-storage solutions.
Motilal Oswal also identifies the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana as a potential demand driver, alongside proposed domestic content requirements for inverters and batteries under the scheme's next phase.

docs.title: Winning the Next Cart: How Shoppers Choose Stores
docs.text:
Consumers don’t want to do a lot of research and make a lot of decisions anytime they make a routine purchase. That’s too much work. Unless there’s a great reason not to, shoppers go to their usual store without much consideration. 
Close to eight in 10 grocery shoppers made their last purchase at their go-to store, and roughly two-thirds did so without comparing prices across merchants. About seven in 10 of those who do compare prices find their store already had the best deal.
Payment options rarely drive shoppers’ merchant choice. Just 1% to 2% of shoppers name payment options as the main reason they chose the store. Still, 29% say those options influenced or determined their choice. Among millennials, that figure climbs to 41%.
These are just some of the findings explored in “ Winning the Next Cart: How Shoppers Choose Stores ,” the latest installment of How People Shop and Pay , a PYMNTS Intelligence exclusive series. This edition is based on a survey of 2,102 U.S. adults conducted from Sept. 11–27, 2026. It examines how consumers decide where to shop. Turns out, it’s usually a matter of habit and convenience, with some key exceptions. 
Complete the form below for free, unlimited access to all our Data Studies, Trackers, and PYMNTS Intelligence reports.
Thank you for registering. Please confirm your email to view all our reports.
When consumers are shopping for groceries, they usually stick to their routine. Seventy-eight percent of shoppers’ most recent grocery purchases were completed at their main grocery store. Just 2% went to a new store or one they couldn’t recall. Meanwhile, people are more likely to branch out for retail. Sixty-one percent of shoppers’ latest retail purchases were made at their main store, while 33% went to a familiar store that wasn’t their primary store. 
These findings are in line with how shoppers describe their overall habits, not just their most recent purchases. When asked how they choose where to buy groceries, 36% said they always or usually go with their preferred store. These shoppers are the self-described loyalists. Meanwhile, only 28% said they choose based on the best deal. These are, accordingly, the deal seekers. In retail, the shares of loyalists and deal seekers are roughly equal, at 30% each.
Among grocery loyalists, 85% made their last purchase at their main store, versus just 71% of deal seekers. In retail, the gap is wider, at 77% versus 53%, respectively. Overall, it seems retailers have to work harder than grocers to win shoppers’ loyalty every time, especially when targeting younger generations. 
Younger generations are less tied to a single store. Among baby boomers and seniors, preferred-store shoppers outnumber deal seekers by 12 points, at 37% versus 25%. Among millennials and Gen Z, that gap shrinks to roughly 4 to 5 points.
Similarly, 66% of baby boomers and seniors went back to their main store for their last retail purchase, compared with just 53% of Gen Z. Gen Z shoppers were also more than twice as likely as baby boomers and seniors to say their most recent purchase was at a store they’d never been to before or one they can’t remember. 
Budget pressures also factor in. Among grocery shoppers who don’t live paycheck to paycheck, 39% tend to choose their preferred store, while 26% prioritize the best deal. Among those living paycheck to paycheck and struggling to pay bills, the gap narrows to 36% versus 30%.
However, financially constrained consumers are somewhat counterintuitively more likely than others to have made their most recent retail purchase at their usual spot. Two-thirds of consumers living paycheck to paycheck and struggling to pay bills went back to their primary merchant, compared with 57% of shoppers who don’t live paycheck to paycheck. It may be that the former category has fewer options when deciding where to shop because of their economic limitations.
Before their most recent grocery purchase, just 32% of shoppers compared prices with another store. Moreover, 38% didn’t check prices at all, not even at the store they ultimately picked. Retail shoppers were even less likely to compare. Twenty-nine percent compared prices across multiple stores, and 43% didn’t check prices at all.
Comparison is far more common among younger and financially stretched shoppers. In groceries, 46% of Gen Z and 43% of millennials compared prices with another store, compared with 26% of Gen X and 19% of baby boomers and seniors. Additionally, 36% of grocery shoppers who live paycheck to paycheck and struggle to pay bills compared prices, versus just 26% of those who don’t live paycheck to paycheck. 
Unsurprisingly, deal seekers are more likely than loyalists to compare. Twenty-seven percent of deal seekers skipped checking prices, versus 40% of loyalists.
Price comparing may become more common over time. The share of consumers reporting frequent cash-flow shortfalls (meaning they often or always ran short of money for living expenses or emergencies in the previous 90 days) reached 19% of consumers in 2026. That’s up from 15% in 2024 and 17% in 2025. If the trend holds, more shoppers may need to start checking prices before they buy.
Roughly seven in 10 shoppers who compared prices found that their chosen store had the best price. Another 17% found prices about the same, and 11% saw a lower price elsewhere but bought from their chosen store anyway.
Age factors in, too. Among grocery shoppers who compared prices, 82% of baby boomers and seniors found their store had the best price, compared with 65% of Gen Z. Still, 16% of price-comparing Gen Z grocery shoppers and 19% of price-comparing Gen Z retail shoppers bought from their chosen store even though another was cheaper. 
For these shoppers, factors other than price, such as convenience or product, appear to carry the decision.
